title: Hyperparameter Tuning with Optuna

blocks.t: From the notes
Hyperparameter tuning, as written

Parameters are learned by the model (the weights). Hyper
parameters are set by us before training — max_depth,
learning_rate, C, k.

GridSearchCV — tries every combination. Guaranteed to find
the best point in the grid, but very slow — the cost is the
product of all the lists.

RandomizedSearchCV — samples n_iter random combinations.
Much faster, and usually just as good.

Optuna — uses Bayesian optimisation: it learns from
the previous trials and tries values that are likely to be better. It
can also prune bad trials early.

Always tune using cross-validation, and keep a separate test
set that tuning never sees.
Why random beats grid

blocks.cap:
The same 25-trial budget spent three ways on a surface where the
horizontal axis matters and the vertical one does not. Grid tests only 5
distinct values of the parameter that counts; random tests 25; TPE spends its
later trials near the optimum.

blocks.t:
The geometry argument (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012). A $5\times5$ grid
over two parameters costs 25 trials, but projects onto only 5 distinct
values of each parameter. In $d$ dimensions a grid with $m$ points per axis
costs $m^d$ trials while still exploring only $m$ values of the one parameter
that actually matters. Random search with $n$ trials explores $n$ distinct
values of every parameter.

There is also a probabilistic guarantee. If the top $p$ fraction of the space is
"good enough", then $n$ random trials miss it with probability $(1-p)^n$. For
the top 5%,

so 60 random trials find a top-5% configuration with 95%
probability, regardless of how many dimensions there are. Grid search offers no
such guarantee at any fixed budget.
The effective dimensionality argument

Real objective functions have a low effective dimension: two or three
hyperparameters dominate and the rest barely register. Grid search spends its
budget uniformly across all of them and therefore wastes most of it. This is why
grid search is defensible only when you have $\le2$ parameters with a handful of
genuinely discrete values — and never otherwise.
How Optuna's TPE sampler works

Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. After some random startup trials,
split the completed trials at a quantile $\gamma$ of the objective and fit two
kernel density estimates:
Then choose the next $x$ to maximise the ratio
\boxed{ x^{\star} = \arg\max_x \frac{\ell(x)}{g(x)} }

which can be shown to be equivalent to maximising Expected
Improvement. Intuitively: sample where good trials have clustered and bad
trials have not.

Note the inversion relative to classical Bayesian optimisation. A Gaussian
process models $p(\text{score}\mid x)$ — the score given the parameters. TPE
models $p(x\mid \text{score})$ — the parameters given the score. The TPE
version scales far better with dimension, handles categorical and conditional
parameters naturally, and costs $O(n)$ per suggestion rather than the GP's
$O(n^3)$.

blocks.cap:
Left: the two densities TPE maintains. Middle: their ratio, whose

blocks.t: Define-by-run search spaces
Optuna's actual innovation

The search space is not a dictionary declared up front — it is written in
ordinary Python inside the objective function, and evaluated afresh on
every trial. That makes conditional search spaces trivial:
if kernel == "rbf": gamma = trial.suggest_float(...)

With GridSearchCV you would have to enumerate a list of
disjoint parameter dictionaries; with Optuna the if statement is the
search space. You can put loops, function calls, and early returns in there
too — it is just code.

head: Suggest method
Use for
rows: Scale parameters: learning_rate, C, alpha, gamma. Anything spanning orders of magnitude

blocks.t:
Use log=True for every scale parameter. A learning rate
sampled uniformly on $[0.001, 0.3]$ puts 99.7% of its samples above $0.001$
and essentially never explores the small end — but the interesting behaviour
is spread evenly across orders of magnitude, not across the linear range.
Log-uniform sampling is the correct prior for anything whose natural comparison
is a ratio. This single flag routinely matters more than the choice of sampler.
Pruning

blocks.cap:
Left: fANOVA parameter importances from the 45-trial study. Middle: a
slice plot for the learning rate. Right: the measured effect of median pruning
on the same 25-trial budget.

blocks.t:
A trial that is clearly worse than the median at fold 1 of 5, or at boosting
round 50 of 500, is very unlikely to win. Pruning stops it there and gives the
budget to the next candidate. You report an intermediate value with
trial.report(value, step), then ask trial.should_prune().

Pruners: MedianPruner (stop if below the median of previous
trials at this step — the safe default), SuccessiveHalvingPruner and
HyperbandPruner (allocate budget in rounds, promoting only the top
performers — best for very large budgets), PatientPruner (wait for
sustained underperformance, useful when learning curves are noisy).

The catch: pruning biases the search towards configurations that are good
early. A small learning rate with many trees looks bad at round 50 and
excellent at round 2000. Set n_warmup_steps generously to protect
slow starters.
Keeping the score honest

The tuned CV score is optimistically biased. You selected the
configuration that scored best on those folds, so that score includes the
maximum of a lot of noise — selection bias, the same effect as the
"winner's curse". With 200 trials the inflation can be one to three
percentage points.

Two fixes. (1) Hold out a test set before tuning begins and touch it
exactly once, at the end. (2) Use nested cross-validation: an inner
loop tunes, an outer loop scores. Nested CV gives an unbiased estimate of "the
whole tuning procedure", not of one particular configuration, and it costs
$k_{\text{outer}}\times k_{\text{inner}}\times n_{\text{trials}}$ fits — which
is why the single held-out test set is what most people use.

Preprocessing must live inside the CV loop. Scaling, imputation,
feature selection and resampling all learn from data. Fitting them on the full
training set before cross-validating leaks the validation folds into the
transform. Wrap everything in a Pipeline and cross-validate the pipeline.
Code

import numpy as np
import optuna
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, cross_val_score,
                                     StratifiedKFold, GridSearchCV,
                                     RandomizedSearchCV)
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=8000, n_features=25, n_informative=10,
                           flip_y=0.03, random_state=0)
# Hold out a test set BEFORE tuning. It is touched exactly once, at the end.
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2,
                                      stratify=y, random_state=0)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE THREE APPROACHES, SAME BUDGET
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
grid = {"n_estimators": [100, 300, 500],
        "max_depth":    [5, 10, None],
        "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10]}          # 27 combinations
gs = GridSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=2),
                  grid, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("grid  :", round(gs.best_score_, 4), gs.best_params_)

from scipy.stats import randint, uniform
rs = RandomizedSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0, n_jobs=2),
                        {"n_estimators": randint(100, 600),
                         "max_depth": randint(3, 25),
                         "min_samples_leaf": randint(1, 20),
                         "max_features": uniform(0.2, 0.8)},
                        n_iter=27, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc",
                        random_state=0, n_jobs=4).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("random:", round(rs.best_score_, 4), rs.best_params_)

# ==================================================================
# 2. OPTUNA -- the objective is just a function that returns a number
# ==================================================================
def objective(trial):
    params = dict(
        n_estimators      = trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 100, 1500),
        num_leaves        = trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 8, 256, log=True),
        learning_rate     = trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.3, log=True),
        min_child_samples = trial.suggest_int("min_child_samples", 5, 100),
        subsample         = trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.5, 1.0),
        subsample_freq    = 1,            # LightGBM ignores subsample without this
        colsample_bytree  = trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.4, 1.0),
        reg_alpha         = trial.suggest_float("reg_alpha",  1e-8, 10.0, log=True),
        reg_lambda        = trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-8, 10.0, log=True),
    )
    model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**params, n_jobs=2, verbose=-1, random_state=0)
    return cross_val_score(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv,
                           scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=2).mean()

study = optuna.create_study(
    direction    = "maximize",
    sampler      = optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=42, n_startup_trials=15),
    pruner       = optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_startup_trials=5, n_warmup_steps=2),
    study_name   = "lgbm_tuning",
    storage      = None,          # "sqlite:///opt.db" to persist and resume
    load_if_exists = True,
)
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=60, timeout=600, n_jobs=1,
               show_progress_bar=False)
print("optuna:", round(study.best_value, 4))
print("params:", study.best_params)

# ==================================================================
# 3. FINAL, HONEST EVALUATION -- the test set, used once
# ==================================================================
final = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**study.best_params, subsample_freq=1,
                           n_jobs=4, verbose=-1, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("tuned CV :", round(study.best_value, 4), "  <- optimistically biased")
print("held-out :", round(roc_auc_score(yte, final.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))
# The gap between these two numbers IS the selection bias from tuning.

# ==================================================================
# 4. CONDITIONAL SEARCH SPACES -- the define-by-run advantage
# ==================================================================
def svm_objective(trial):
    kernel = trial.suggest_categorical("kernel", ["linear", "rbf", "poly"])
    params = {"C": trial.suggest_float("C", 1e-3, 1e3, log=True), "kernel": kernel}
    if kernel in ("rbf", "poly"):                       # only sampled if relevant
        params["gamma"] = trial.suggest_float("gamma", 1e-5, 1e1, log=True)
    if kernel == "poly":
        params["degree"] = trial.suggest_int("degree", 2, 5)
        params["coef0"]  = trial.suggest_float("coef0", 0.0, 2.0)
    pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("svm", SVC(**params))])
    return cross_val_score(pipe, Xtr[:2000], ytr[:2000], cv=3,
                           scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=2).mean()

svm_study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
                                sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0))
svm_study.optimize(svm_objective, n_trials=30, show_progress_bar=False)
print("SVM best:", svm_study.best_params)
# GridSearchCV would need a LIST of disjoint dicts to express this.

# ==================================================================
# 5. PRUNING -- report intermediate values, ask whether to stop
# ==================================================================
def pruned_objective(trial):
    lr = trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.3, log=True)
    nl = trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 8, 200, log=True)
    scores = []
    for step, (tr_i, va_i) in enumerate(cv.split(Xtr, ytr)):
        m = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=lr, num_leaves=nl,
                               n_jobs=2, verbose=-1, random_state=0)
        m.fit(Xtr[tr_i], ytr[tr_i])
        scores.append(roc_auc_score(ytr[va_i], m.predict_proba(Xtr[va_i])[:, 1]))

        trial.report(float(np.mean(scores)), step)      # tell Optuna how it's going
        if trial.should_prune():                        # ...and let it stop you
            raise optuna.TrialPruned()
    return float(np.mean(scores))

pstudy = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
            pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_startup_trials=5, n_warmup_steps=1))
pstudy.optimize(pruned_objective, n_trials=40, show_progress_bar=False)
n_pruned = sum(t.state == optuna.trial.TrialState.PRUNED for t in pstudy.trials)
print(f"{n_pruned} of {len(pstudy.trials)} trials pruned early")

# ==================================================================
# 6. UNDERSTANDING THE STUDY
# ==================================================================
imp = optuna.importance.get_param_importances(study)   # fANOVA
for k, v in imp.items():
    print(f"{k:20s} {v:.4f}")
# Drop the parameters at the bottom and re-run with a tighter range around the
# top ones -- this is how you get the most out of a second tuning pass.

df = study.trials_dataframe()          # every trial as a pandas DataFrame
print(df[["number", "value", "state"]].tail())

# Visualisations (need plotly):
#   optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_slice(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_parallel_coordinate(study)
#   optuna.visualization.plot_contour(study, params=["learning_rate", "num_leaves"])

# ==================================================================
# 7. PRACTICALITIES
# ==================================================================
# Persist and resume / parallelise across machines:
#   study = optuna.create_study(storage="sqlite:///study.db",
#                               study_name="run1", load_if_exists=True)
#   ...then launch the same script in several processes; they share the study.
#
# Multi-objective (accuracy AND latency):
#   study = optuna.create_study(directions=["maximize", "minimize"])
#   return auc, inference_ms          # gives a Pareto front via study.best_trials
#
# Warm start from configurations you already trust:
#   study.enqueue_trial({"learning_rate": 0.05, "num_leaves": 31})

# ==================================================================
# 8. NESTED CV -- the unbiased (expensive) estimate
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score as cvs
outer = StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
scores = []
for tr_i, te_i in outer.split(X, y):
    inner_study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
                    sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0))
    Xi, yi = X[tr_i], y[tr_i]
    inner_study.optimize(lambda t: cvs(
        lgb.LGBMClassifier(
            learning_rate=t.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-3, 0.3, log=True),
            num_leaves=t.suggest_int("num_leaves", 8, 128, log=True),
            n_estimators=300, n_jobs=2, verbose=-1, random_state=0),
        Xi, yi, cv=3, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=2).mean(),
        n_trials=15, show_progress_bar=False)
    best = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**inner_study.best_params, n_estimators=300,
                              n_jobs=4, verbose=-1, random_state=0).fit(Xi, yi)
    scores.append(roc_auc_score(y[te_i], best.predict_proba(X[te_i])[:, 1]))
print("nested CV:", np.round(scores, 4), "mean", round(np.mean(scores), 4))
Everything on one page
Summary

Grid tries every combination — cost is the product of the lists, and
$m^d$ trials still explore only $m$ values per parameter. Use it only for
$\le2$ genuinely discrete parameters.

Random explores $n$ distinct values of every parameter and finds
a top-5% configuration with 95% probability in 60 trials, independent of
dimension.

Optuna / TPE models $\ell(x)$ (good trials) and $g(x)$ (bad trials) and
samples where $\ell/g$ is largest — equivalent to maximising Expected
Improvement. Cheap, handles categoricals and conditionals, scales with
dimension.

Define-by-run: the search space is Python inside the objective, so
conditional parameters are just if statements.

Always log=True for learning rates, regularisation strengths,
$C$, $\gamma$ — anything compared by ratio.

Honesty: the tuned CV score is optimistically biased. Hold out a test
set before tuning and use it once, or run nested CV. Keep all preprocessing
inside the pipeline.

Order of operations: pick the metric $\to$ build a correct CV split
$\to$ get a baseline $\to$ tune the 2–3 parameters that matter (check
get_param_importances) $\to$ re-tune in a narrower range $\to$ evaluate
once on the test set.
Interview corner
Q. Why is random search usually better than grid search?

Because objective functions have low effective dimensionality — only a few
hyperparameters matter. A grid spends its budget uniformly and projects onto few
distinct values per parameter, while random search gives $n$ distinct values of
every parameter for the same $n$ trials. It also scales to any dimension without
the combinatorial explosion.
Q. How many random trials do you need?

$1-(1-p)^n$ is the probability of hitting the top-$p$ fraction. For the top 5%
with 95% confidence, $n=60$ — independent of the number of hyperparameters.
Q. How does Bayesian optimisation differ from random search?

It builds a probabilistic model of the objective from completed trials and uses
it to choose the next point, balancing exploitation (near known good regions)
with exploration (where the model is uncertain). Random search never learns; its
$n$th trial is as uninformed as its first.
Q. Explain TPE.

Split completed trials into a good group and a bad group at a quantile, fit a
kernel density to each — $\ell(x)$ and $g(x)$ — and sample the candidate
maximising $\ell(x)/g(x)$, which is equivalent to Expected Improvement. Unlike a
Gaussian process it models $p(x\mid\text{score})$ rather than
$p(\text{score}\mid x)$, so it costs $O(n)$ per suggestion and handles
categorical and conditional parameters naturally.
Q. What is pruning and what is its risk?

Stopping unpromising trials early using intermediate scores (fold-by-fold or
epoch-by-epoch). The risk is bias towards configurations that look good early:
a small learning rate with many iterations is slow to start and may be killed
before it wins. Use enough warmup steps.
Q. Why sample the learning rate on a log scale?

Because it is a scale parameter — 0.001 to 0.01 is as meaningful a change as
0.01 to 0.1. Uniform sampling on $[0.001,0.3]$ would almost never test the small
end. Log-uniform gives equal probability to each order of magnitude.
Q. Why is the best CV score from tuning biased?

Because you selected the maximum over many noisy estimates, so the winner
includes a favourable draw of noise. The more trials, the larger the inflation.
Report a held-out test score or use nested CV instead.
Q. When is nested CV worth its cost?

When the dataset is small (so a single held-out split is high-variance), when
you must publish an unbiased estimate of the whole modelling procedure, or when
comparing two tuning strategies fairly. For large data, one untouched test set
is cheaper and adequate.
Q. How do you tune when a single fit takes hours?

Tune on a stratified subsample or a subset of features first to localise the
good region, use aggressive pruning (Hyperband), reduce the CV folds during
search and validate properly only at the end, warm-start with known-good
configurations via enqueue_trial, and parallelise across machines with a
shared storage backend.
Q. Which parameters should you actually tune?

Check get_param_importances after a first pass. For gradient boosting:
learning rate and number of trees together, then tree complexity
(num_leaves/max_depth, min_child_samples), then
sampling and regularisation. Tuning everything at once with a small budget is
worse than tuning the top three well.
Worked Examples
Why the search space should be log-scaled
Search a learning rate in $[0.001,\;0.1]$.
Uniform sampling. The chance a draw lands below $0.01$ is
Only 9% of trials explore the small-rate region, although the two decades $[0.001,0.01]$ and $[0.01,0.1]$ are equally important on a log scale.
Log-uniform sampling. Draw $\log_{10}(\text{lr})$ uniformly on $[-3,-1]$:
Each decade gets equal attention. The geometric midpoint is $\sqrt{0.001\cdot 0.1} = 0.01$, while the arithmetic midpoint $0.0505$ is far from it.

How Optuna uses trials. It samples with a configured distribution (suggest_float(..., log=True)), records each (parameters, score), and models which regions score well (TPE). Later trials concentrate near the best region found so far, so a grid of 12 trials covers 12 fixed points while 12 Optuna trials can converge on a good value.
Pruning. MedianPruner stops a trial early if its intermediate score is worse than the median of earlier trials at the same step, saving compute.
